bot:
A pressure-independent control valve (PICV) combines a flow-limiting cartridge with a modulating control valve in one body. Unlike a standard control valve, it holds the flow rate you set regardless of pressure swings elsewhere in the system — so you don't need a separate balancing valve, and flow stays accurate even as other zones open and close.
VRN Pressure Independent Control Valves — Specification Data, Form 62-3115 ↗

A valve's connection size and its rated flow range are linked — each body size is engineered to control accurately across a specific flow band. A 4-inch PICV in this catalog is rated roughly 55+ GPM; running it far below that range, like 5 GPM, means the flow-limiting cartridge can't regulate precisely, so the valve won't reliably hold its setpoint. That's why matching body size to actual flow rate matters more than matching it to the pipe size alone.

bot: Fail-safe action defines what the actuator does if it loses power or its control signal: fail-in-place holds the valve at its last position, fail-safe closed drives it fully shut, and fail-safe open drives it fully open.

Here's the trade-off in more detail: with fail-in-place, if power or the control signal is ever lost, the valve simply stays wherever it was — flow keeps moving, just without active control until power's restored. With fail-safe closed, that same loss drives the valve fully shut, so cooling to both presses stops immediately.

Neither is 'safer' in the abstract — it depends which failure mode your team would rather manage: an uncontrolled-but-flowing loop, or a hard stop that could trigger a shutdown or scrap on the presses.
